extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of social theory / political economy (general educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate analogies between individual organisms and societies — e.g., stages of differentiation, circulation/distribution systems, nervous/governmental organization, and indicators (money, roads, markets) that mark levels of social complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary differentiation: governing vs governed
rubrics_metrics.description: The only manifest contrast of parts in primitive societies is that between the governing and the governed; this primary differentiation is the first stage of social evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functionally, the governing class corresponds to organs of external action (war, negotiation, migration) while the governed (inferior) class corresponds to organs of nutrition. Examples: primitive chiefs distinguished by courage/experience; later forming freemen and slaves or nobles and serfs. Note that this is the broad general distinction rather than a rigorous absolute; some organs/classes may involve mixed functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergence of an intermediate (trading/middle) class
rubrics_metrics.description: Between the governing and governed arises a trading or middle class analogous to the vascular layer, whose members act as distributors transferring commodities from producers to consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wholesale and retail dealers are agents of transfer, collecting and dividing commodities; their intermediate origin, position, and time of appearance parallel the vascular layer of embryos. Observe presence/absence of such distributors as an indicator of social development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of differentiation: from general to specific
rubrics_metrics.description: The most general and broadly contrasted divisions appear first; subdivisions arise in the order of decreasing generality — specializations are at first incomplete and grow more definite with progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In primitive societies many functions are shared (e.g., chiefs performing many roles); as society advances, roles (church, state, military, handicrafts) separate and become more specialized. Use historical examples (kings originally as landowners, bishops as military leaders) to illustrate transitional, vague specializations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fusion and obliteration of original boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: As small communities coalesce into larger societies, original lines of separation (segments, local organizations) gradually lose external/internaI distinctness; sustaining organizations traverse old boundaries while governmental/co-ordinating structures retain traces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare segmented organisms (Annulosa) with fusion in Crustacea; in societies, feudal communities merge under central power so county/parish boundaries become less relevant to economic organization (e.g., industrial regions crossing county lines). The presence of sustaining systems that ignore older limits is diagnostic of higher integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth requires surplus (profit analogous to nutrition surplus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth of an organ or social part follows greater functional activity only if nutrition (blood / commodities) supplied exceeds waste; in commerce, profit corresponds to excess of nutrition over waste and enables expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If increased production only replaces expenditure and wear, there is no growth; surplus returned as commodities (profit) fuels enlargement. Conversely, excessive activity with deficient nutrition leads to atrophy/decay (bankruptcy, decline). Use balance of inputs/outputs as a growth criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition among parts for nutritive resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Different parts of a social organism compete for nutriment (commodities/capital) and obtain more or less according to how much duty/activity they discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: an overexcited brain abstracts blood from viscera; similarly, development of railways or raising a large military force can abstract capital and temporarily arrest other economic activities. Track shifts of capital/commodities to identify competitive prioritization within a society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulating mass composition becomes more elaborate and heterogeneous
rubrics_metrics.description: As division of labour increases, the circulating stream of commodities becomes of superior 'quality' (more elaborated products) and more heterogeneous in composition, analogous to blood varying across animal grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater specialization among producers yields more complex and varied merchandize flows. Empirical confirmation (per Dr. Williams) shows blood heterogeneity across animal grades; likewise, examine variety/complexity of traded goods as index of social complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance of money as a non-nutritive facilitating element
rubrics_metrics.description: At a certain stage of organization, money appears in the social circulation performing the function of blood-corpuscles: not consumed in nutrition but facilitating exchange and activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liebig's analogy: coin circulates extensively without being consumed, enabling large currents of commerce. The absence of money indicates low civilization; its quantity and turnover in mercantile centers signals advanced organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development of channels of communication parallels vascular evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribution channels progress from mere tracks/lacunae to definite roads with lined walls (blood-vessels); main channels become broad and straight while subordinate ones remain narrow and tortuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early societies have tracks/trails for occasional exchange; with progress, roads are fenced/gravelled and transport infrastructure resembles arteries and veins, including double channels (railways) for bidirectional flow. Evaluate physical infrastructure (road/rail networks) to assess circulatory sophistication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rates and rhythms of circulation reflect organizational stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulatory movement evolves from slow, irregular gurgitations/regurgitations (periodic fairs) to steady, rapid, regular pulses (daily markets and frequent transfers), mirroring the shift from local variable currents to permanent directed circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe frequency of markets (fairs → weekly → daily → multiple times per day) and transport velocities (parish roads → high roads → main lines/railways) as indicators of maturity of distribution systems; centrality shows stronger pulses while periphery retains slower, irregular flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation of directive and executive agencies (nervous/governmental analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Directive (deliberative) and executive (coercive) functions are initially mingled in ruling classes but become distinct as societies grow; this parallels ectoderm differentiation into impressible (intelligence) and contractile (strength) units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In early tribes chiefs both direct and execute; in larger societies, rulers delegate execution and assume roles requiring cunning, foresight, and management skill rather than mere physical strength. Use presence of separate legislative, judicial, and military bodies as evidence of this differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributors as part of the circulating apparatus, occupying intermediate position
rubrics_metrics.description: Wholesale and retail distributors discharge the office of the vascular system: they appear later than primary classes, occupy an intermediate position, and together with channels constitute the complete social circulation system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete conception of social circulation includes both human agents propelling commodity currents and the physical channels they use. Evaluate both classes of actors and infrastructure to understand distribution efficiency and development.
